race.name: GFNY Colonia
race.tagline: One hundred twenty-five rolling kilometers where the Río San Juan rise and Uruguay River wind decide who still has a group.

vitals.start_format: Mass-start competitive long course with chip timing
vitals.registration: Online through the official GFNY race site
vitals.feed_zones: Official GFNY aid stations with hydration, food, technical, and medical support
vitals.cutoff_time: See current race guide and official course rules

climate.description: GFNY identifies the usual coastal wind as a defining race factor. The open Route 21 terrain offers limited shelter, so direction and group position can change the cost of the same speed.

terrain.surface: Paved Route 21 and surrounding roads through fields, olive groves, vineyards, and riverfront settlements.
features: A fast rolling opening on Route 21
The Río San Juan rise around kilometer 36
Long exposed sections where wind shapes the peloton
A compact-race profile without a single major mountain

fondo_rating.scoring_notes: An established GFNY long course with real distance, wind-driven tactics, and strong destination character. Moderate climbing keeps it below the hardest flagship fondos.

key_climbs: Río San Juan rise near kilometer 36
climb_profile.king_of_mountain: The Río San Juan rise is the named selection point, but the more persistent challenge is holding useful position in the coastal wind.

course_description.character: The competitive route uses 125 kilometers of rolling riverfront terrain with 900 meters of climbing. The field can stay compact until the Río San Juan rise, after which exposed roads and coastal wind reward riders who can preserve a group and repeat short efforts without wasting energy.
course_description.signature_challenge: The combination of the Río San Juan rise and the wind-exposed roads that follow.

logistics.airport: Carrasco International Airport (MVD) is Uruguay's main international gateway; Buenos Aires also connects to Colonia by ferry.
logistics.lodging_strategy: Stay in or near Colonia del Sacramento and confirm race-morning access in the current race guide.
logistics.transport: Use official race-week instructions for packet pickup, start access, and bike transport.
logistics.food: Colonia has restaurants and markets, but carry familiar race nutrition because the long course is exposed and group speed can make early feeding easy to postpone.

history.origin_story: GFNY's Colonia event established a competitive long route through Uruguay's historic riverfront countryside.
notable_moments: 2025: Official race guide and results establish the current event
history.reputation: A tactical rolling-road GFNY where wind and group decisions matter more than a headline mountain.

biased_opinion.summary: Colonia is not a climbing monster, which is exactly why it can punish sloppy riders. The first decisive rise arrives early enough to split the field, and every exposed kilometer afterward makes group choice, feeding, and wind awareness expensive to get wrong.
strengths: Manageable climbing with real race tactics
weaknesses: Course difficulty depends heavily on wind
Few major climbs for mountain-focused riders
International travel can require a ferry or long transfer
biased_opinion.bottom_line: Choose Colonia for a real rolling road race where the right group is worth more than one heroic climb.

final_verdict.one_liner: One hundred twenty-five rolling kilometers where the Río San Juan rise and Uruguay River wind decide who still has a group.
final_verdict.should_you_race: Choose Colonia for a real rolling road race where the right group is worth more than one heroic climb.
final_verdict.alternatives: GFNY José Ignacio for Atlantic heat and a longer coastal sector, or GFNY Punta del Este for more climbing.

source_review.facts_scope: Date, competitive status, long- and medium-course distance and elevation, and named course features verified against first-party GFNY sources.
